paper_metadata.title: Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks with Amplitude Encoding for Credit Recovery Rate Prediction

summary: The paper proposes a hybrid QML regression model using amplitude encoding (256 features → 8 qubits) for bond recovery‑rate prediction on 1,725 observations. The amplitude‑encoded model achieves RMSE 0.228, outperforming a classical FNN baseline (0.246) and an angle‑encoded QML model (0.242), but remains slightly worse than XGBoost (0.222) in cross‑validation. All main experiments are executed on an 8‑qubit noiseless state‑vector simulator.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum machine learning model for recovery rate prediction using a classical preprocessing layer followed by an amplitude-encoded parameterized quantum circuit, evaluated on a 256-feature credit recovery dataset against FNN, angle-encoded QML, and XGBoost baselines.

algorithm.variant: hybrid QML with amplitude encoding and strongly entangling PQC
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained for 100 epochs; best average RMSE selected from cross-validation/LOOCV

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 256 classical features are amplitude-encoded into an 8-qubit state (2^8 = 256); classical preprocessing layer first transforms the input before quantum state preparation
problem_formulation.objective_function: regression minimizing RMSE for recovery rate prediction
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: unitary PQC; no explicit penalty formulation

problem_instance.description: Predict bond recovery rate at default using firm-level, bond-level, credit-risk, categorical, and macroeconomic features
problem_instance.dataset_name: NRF Research Project UP5 / CRI-NUS recovery rate dataset

dataset_specification.description: 1,725 observations from 576 firms spanning 1996-2023; recovery amount defined as bond price 30 days after default

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: continuous features standardized with z-score normalization using training set only; categorical True/False features mapped to 0/1; no missing entries in retained variables; no PCA
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: four-fold cross-validation and leave-one-out cross-validation; RMSE tracked per epoch; Diebold-Mariano significance tests across folds/epochs

hardware.device_name: PennyLane default.qubit state‑vector simulator executed on Intel Core i9‑13900H CPU

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; GPU-accelerated PyTorch for FNN/XGBoost baselines
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: classical neural preprocessing layer with input and hidden layer of equal size using LeakyReLU
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: classical output layer for regression on measured quantum expectation values

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: RMSE decreases over epochs; amplitude-encoded model reaches best average RMSE at epoch 55 (CV) and 86 (LOOCV)

speedup_claims.caveats: Paper reports empirical performance comparisons only; no asymptotic quantum speedup is claimed for recovery-rate prediction.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Amplitude encoding state preparation via Möttönen protocol uses 2^(n+1)-3 elementary gates for n qubits; PQC parameter count scales as O(3 log2 N) for N features

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No asymptotic speedup analysis; only 8‑qubit PQC on classical simulator with ~24 variational parameters
limiting_factors: Amplitude encoding requires exponential‑gate state preparation (≈2^(n+1)−3 gates)
Entire experiment performed on noiseless classical simulator
No complexity advantage demonstrated over classical ML
XGBoost baseline achieves lower RMSE in cross‑validation
Data loading via amplitude encoding dominates circuit cost

notes: circuit_depth not explicitly given for the full amplitude-encoded experiment; only the state-preparation gate count and qualitative depth implications are discussed
speedup_order inferred as none_proven because the paper reports empirical performance comparisons but no asymptotic quantum speedup claim for the recovery-rate task
Paper reports QML outperforming FNN (RMSE 0.228 vs 0.246) but XGBoost achieves lower RMSE (0.222) in CV.
Authors explicitly state QML is only competitive with XGBoost, not superior.
